title: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
summary: Reflected, stored and DOM XSS traced from source to sink, encoding by context, sanitisers, CSP and Trusted Types, CSRF and its defences, open redirects, skimmers and extensions.
outcomes: Explain why script injected into a page gets that origin's full power despite the same-origin policy
Trace reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS from source to sink and fix each at the right place
Choose the right encoding for HTML body, attribute, JavaScript and URL contexts, and spot framework escape hatches
Use DOMPurify, a strict CSP and Trusted Types as layered defences, and say what each cannot stop
Explain how browsers attach cookies to forged requests and defend with SameSite, tokens and Fetch Metadata
Validate redirect targets and explain clickjacking, third-party script and browser extension risk

lessons.title: XSS: when your page runs someone else's code

blocks.md:
Picture a shop with a search box. You search for `gift` and the page says **Results for gift**. The server built that page by pasting your words into its HTML. Now someone searches for `<script>alert(1)</script>` instead. If the server pastes those characters in unchanged, the browser reads a script tag, not a product name, and runs it. A pop-up appears. That pop-up is harmless, but it proves that text typed by a stranger became code in the shop's page.

That bug is **cross-site scripting**, XSS. As the prerequisite course noted, a small group of Microsoft engineers settled on the name in 2000, and it is written XSS because CSS already meant Cascading Style Sheets. OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit that publishes free security guidance) calls the name a misnomer: early attacks stole data *across sites*, but today it covers any untrusted content that a page ends up running.

Recall the same-origin policy from the prerequisite: a script from one origin cannot read pages from another. XSS does not break that rule. It walks around it. The injected script is delivered **by the shop's own server, inside the shop's own page**, so the browser files it under `https://shop.example` like every other script there. MDN puts it this way: the attacker tricks the site into running malicious code within its own context, as though it were same-origin.

From inside, the script can do anything the page's real code can. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy (free training from the company behind the Burp Suite testing tool) lists the impact: perform any action the user can, view any data the user can, change any data the user can, and start interactions with other users that look like they came from the victim.

blocks.title: Injected script runs inside the victim's origin

scenes.caption: The attacker cannot read shop.example from their own site: the same-origin policy blocks evil.example's script from reading the shop's responses.
So the attacker hands text to the shop instead: a search term, a comment or a profile field. To the server it is just a string.
The shop pastes the string into HTML without encoding it. The browser receives one page from shop.example and parses the attacker's text as a script tag.
The injected script runs as shop.example. It can read the DOM, including forms and anti-forgery tokens, and localStorage. These are same-origin reads, so nothing blocks them.
It can call fetch() on shop.example. The browser attaches the victim's cookies as it would for any request from the shop's own code, then sends what it learns wherever the attacker likes.

blocks.md: An `HttpOnly` session cookie does not make XSS harmless. It stops script from *reading* the cookie, so the attacker cannot take the session home. But the injected script does not need the cookie value: it sends requests from the victim's own browser, and the browser attaches the cookie for it.

Security people describe every XSS bug with two words. A **source** is where attacker-controlled data enters: a URL parameter, a form field, a stored comment, a message from another window. A **sink** is the place where that data is interpreted: an HTML template, `innerHTML`, `eval()`. OWASP's cheat sheet explains the metaphor: if you pollute a river, it flows downstream somewhere. The bug is any path from a source to a sink that interprets the data as code.

The classic names describe how the data travels:

- **Reflected**: the payload is in the request, and the server copies it straight into its response (lesson 2).
- **Stored**: the server saves the payload and serves it to later visitors (lesson 3).
- **DOM-based**: the page's own JavaScript moves the payload from a source to a sink in the browser (lesson 4).

OWASP adds a useful second axis: *server-side* versus *client-side* says where data was handled unsafely. A stored payload can still end in a client-side sink.

blocks.caption: Two sinks from MDN's XSS guide, and the fix for each (escapeHtml is defined in lesson 2).

blocks.md:
**Defender view, in one line per stage.** *Prevent*: encode or sanitise every value at the point it enters HTML, using your framework's defaults, then add a strict CSP as backup (lessons 5 to 8). *Detect*: CSP violation reports, suspicious markup in request logs, and stored content that contains tags (lesson 14). *Respond*: fix the sink, remove stored payloads, and end sessions that may have been used.

Everything in this course is for understanding and defending. Only test systems you own or have written permission to test.

blocks.question: A shop's product page has an XSS bug. Why can the injected script read the logged-in user's order history from `https://shop.example/api/orders`?
options: The script runs in the shop.example origin, so requests to the shop's own API are same-origin
The same-origin policy is switched off while a script tag is being parsed
XSS payloads always steal the session cookie first, then replay it
Browsers let any script read JSON responses, because JSON is not HTML
blocks.explain: The injected script was delivered inside the shop's page, so the browser treats it as shop.example code. Reading the shop's own API is a same-origin request, and the browser attaches the victim's cookies. No cookie theft and no policy failure is needed.

blocks.question: The session cookie is `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`. An attacker finds stored XSS on the site. What can their script still do?
options: Nothing useful, since it cannot see the session cookie
Only read public pages, because HttpOnly strips cookies from script-initiated requests
Act as the user from inside their browser, such as changing their email, because the browser still attaches the cookie to the script's same-origin requests
Read the cookie by calling document.cookie inside an iframe
blocks.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie value from document.cookie, but requests made by fetch() still carry it. SameSite does not matter either, because the request is same-site. The attacker cannot carry the session to their machine, but they can use it right there.

lessons.title: Reflected XSS: the server echoes the attack back

blocks.md:
**Reflected XSS** happens, in PortSwigger's words, when an application receives data in an HTTP request and includes that data within the immediate response in an unsafe way. *Reflected* because the payload comes straight back in the response to the same request: it is never stored. Tiny example. `https://shop.example/search?q=gift` returns `

Results for gift

`. If the attacker can get a victim to open `https://shop.example/search?q=`, the victim's browser receives `

Results for

` from the real shop, and runs it.

blocks.caption: Run with Express 5 on Node 22. The marker only shows where the input lands; the fix is two blocks below.

blocks.title: A reflected XSS, from link to stolen data

scenes.caption: The attacker cannot inject into the shop directly, so they send the victim a link to the real shop with the payload in a query parameter, by email, chat or a post.
The victim clicks. Their browser sends the request to the genuine shop, with their session cookie attached.
The server copies q into the page without encoding. The response is real shop.example HTML with the attacker's script tag inside it.
The script makes same-origin requests as the victim. The browser attaches the cookie, so the API answers.
Sending data out is a write, which the same-origin policy allows. Without a CSP limiting destinations, nothing stops it.
With the fix, the same request returns the payload as harmless text: the browser displays the characters and runs nothing.

blocks.prompt: The victim clicks the attacker's link while logged out of the shop. What happens?
blocks.reveal: The script still runs, because the server still reflects it. But there is no session to abuse, so it can only do what an anonymous visitor could, unless it waits for the user to log in on that page. PortSwigger points out that this is why reflected XSS is generally less severe than stored XSS: it needs an outside delivery channel and lucky timing, while a stored payload waits inside the application for users who are already logged in.

blocks.caption: The entity table is OWASP's rule for HTML contexts. In real code, prefer your template engine's automatic escaping (lesson 6).

blocks.md:
**Why the fix works.** The browser's HTML parser starts a tag only when it sees a literal `<`. The entity `<` is a *character reference*: the parser turns it into a visible `<` character inside a text node, after the point where it decides what is a tag. So the user sees exactly what they typed, and the structure of the page cannot change. Encoding `&` too matters, otherwise text that already looks like an entity would be decoded.

Note where the fix goes: **at output**, right where data enters HTML. Filtering input is a weaker idea. A filter that deletes the word `script` breaks legitimate searches and still misses the many other ways to start code, as MySpace learned (lesson 3). Validating input is still good hygiene (a quantity must be a number), but OWASP is explicit that it does not replace output encoding.

**Self-XSS** is a cousin worth knowing. The code path is the same, but the payload can only arrive if the victims paste it into the page themselves, for example after being told "paste this into your browser to unlock a feature". PortSwigger rates it low impact because it needs that social engineering.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: auto-escaping templates and no string-built HTML. *Detect*: a reflected payload travels in the request, so it shows up in web server access logs and is visible to a **WAF** (web application firewall: a filter in front of the app that inspects requests). The OWASP Core Rule Set, a widely used open-source WAF rule set, has a family of XSS rules (IDs 941xxx) that flag script tags, event-handler attributes and `javascript:` URLs in parameters. *Respond*: fix the template, search logs for other requests that hit the same parameter with markup, and if the page was sensitive, end the affected sessions.

blocks.question: A developer fixes reflected XSS by deleting `<script>` and `</script>` from the q parameter before storing it in a variable. What is the main problem?
options: Deleting tags is slower than encoding them
It is correct, but should be done in the browser instead of on the server
It breaks HTTPS, because the request no longer matches its signature
Markup can run script without a script tag, for example through an event-handler attribute, so a deny-list of tags leaves the sink open
blocks.explain: A deny-list removes the one form the developer thought of. HTML has many places where script can start, such as event-handler attributes and javascript: URLs. Encoding at output closes them all at once, because no attacker character can start markup.

blocks.question: Which log is most likely to contain evidence of a reflected XSS attempt?
options: The database's slow query log
The web server's access log, since the payload is part of the requested URL
The browser's localStorage
No log: reflected payloads never reach the server
blocks.explain: Reflected XSS needs the server to echo the payload, so the payload must be in the request, usually the query string. Access logs and WAF logs record it. That is not true of DOM XSS through the URL fragment, which never leaves the browser (lesson 4).

lessons.title: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck

blocks.md:
**Stored XSS** (also called *persistent* or *second-order* XSS) is PortSwigger's term for an application that receives data from an untrusted source and includes it in its *later* HTTP responses in an unsafe way. The classic case is a comment: someone posts it once, the site saves it in a database, and every visitor to the page receives it.

Two things make this worse than reflected XSS. The attacker no longer needs to deliver a link to each victim: the application delivers the payload itself. And the victims are, by definition, people using the site, so they are usually logged in.

blocks.caption: Store data as it was typed and encode on output, so the right encoding can be chosen for each place it appears (HTML, email, JSON).

scenes.caption: The attacker submits a comment containing markup. To the server it is just text, and it is saved as-is.
Visitor A loads the post. The server reads the comment and pastes it into the page without encoding, so A's browser runs it as shop.example.
Visitors B and C load the same page and get the same script. Nobody had to click a strange link; they just read comments while logged in.
Worm step: the script uses each visitor's session to post a copy of itself. Now the database holds many payloads and each new page view spreads it further.
With output encoding, the same stored text reaches visitors as visible characters. The database still holds the attacker's text, but it never runs.

blocks.md:
**Real case: the Samy worm (MySpace, October 2005).** MySpace was then the largest social network, and profiles allowed some HTML so people could decorate them. Samy Kamkar, then 19, released a profile containing hidden script around midnight on 4 October 2005. Kamkar's technical write-up shows that MySpace defended with string filters: it allowed only a few tags (``, ``, `
` and a few others), and a **deny-list** stripped `

The script then did what any page code can do. It read the viewer's page to find their ID, requested their profile to read their list of "heroes", and made requests as the viewer to add Kamkar as a friend. MySpace protected that action with a random hash on a confirmation page, a form of anti-forgery token, but the script simply requested the confirmation page first, read the hash out of it (a same-origin read) and sent it back. Finally it wrote "but most of all, samy is my hero" and a copy of itself into the viewer's own profile, so everyone who viewed *that* profile was infected too.

The prerequisite course showed the one wrinkle: profiles were served from `profile.myspace.com` but the actions lived on `www.myspace.com`, so the script first reloaded the page on `www` to be same-origin.

blocks.title: Samy worm: friend requests waiting, from Kamkar's own log

scenes.caption: 4 October 2005. One hour after release, one request. Each infected profile infects its own viewers, so growth compounds.
By 8:35 am, 221 requests. By 10:30 am, 561. On a linear scale these bars are still invisible next to what follows.
By 1:30 pm, 6,373 requests, and people were being re-infected as soon as they removed Kamkar, by viewing any infected profile.
By 6:20 pm, 917,084, and minutes later 1,005,831: over a million users in under 20 hours. Then MySpace took the site down to remove the worm.

blocks.md:
Kamkar wrote that every request came from a unique, logged-in user. MySpace went offline that evening. According to a retrospective by [Vice Motherboard](https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-myspace-worm-that-changed-the-internet-forever/), Kamkar later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three years of probation with almost no computer access.

**Real case: the TweetDeck worm (11 June 2014).** TweetDeck was Twitter's dashboard app. A 19-year-old in Austria who gave only the name Florian told Threatpost that a tweet containing a Unicode heart character was not HTML-escaped by TweetDeck (the heart was swapped for an image, and that path skipped escaping). Florian confirmed it with a `<strong>` tag and tweeted it publicly. Within hours someone wrote a tweet whose script made TweetDeck retweet it automatically; the Guardian, quoted by [NPR](https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2014/06/11/321019050/tweetdeck-vulnerability-opens-user-accounts-to-hackers), reported it spread 38,000 times in two minutes. TweetDeck shipped a fix, then went offline for about an hour when it did not hold.

Both worms are stored XSS that spread because the payload could use the victim's session to store itself again. Both trace back to a gap in **output encoding**: a filter that guessed at browser parsing (MySpace) and one rendering path that skipped escaping (TweetDeck). Encoding has to happen on every path, as the very last step before data enters HTML.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: encode on output everywhere a stored value is shown, including obscure screens: PortSwigger's example is a display name that also appears in an audit log only some users can see. Uploaded files are stored content too: an SVG or HTML file served inline from your origin runs its script, so serve uploads from a separate domain with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. *Detect*: a stored payload produces the same CSP violation report from many different users on the same page, which is a strong signal (lesson 14); a scheduled search of user-generated content for tags or `javascript:` finds planted payloads. *Respond*: as MySpace and TweetDeck did, disable the feature or take it offline, fix the rendering, remove every stored copy (worms leave thousands), and invalidate sessions, since each infected visitor's account may have been used.

blocks.question: MySpace required a random hash from a confirmation page before adding a friend. Why did that not stop the Samy worm?
options: The hash was the same for every user, so it could be hard-coded
The worm guessed the hash by brute force
MySpace forgot to check the hash on the server
The worm's script ran inside MySpace's origin, so it could request the confirmation page, read the hash and submit it
blocks.explain: Anti-forgery tokens stop requests from other sites, which cannot read the token. Script injected into the site's own origin can read any same-origin page, so it reads the token like the real page would. OWASP's CSRF cheat sheet states it directly: XSS can defeat all CSRF mitigations.

blocks.question: A site stores comments exactly as typed and encodes them when rendering the blog page. A new admin dashboard shows the latest comments using a different template that does not encode. What is the risk?
options: Stored XSS that runs in administrators' browsers, with administrator privileges
None, because the comments were safe on the blog page
Only the attacker sees the payload, so it is self-XSS
The database will reject the comment the second time it is read
blocks.explain: Safety is a property of each output path, not of the stored data. The dashboard is a new sink, and its viewers have the most powerful sessions in the system, which makes this one of the worst places for stored XSS.

lessons.title: DOM-based XSS: when the bug lives in your JavaScript

blocks.md:
In reflected and stored XSS the server writes the dangerous HTML. In **DOM-based XSS** the server may send a perfectly safe page, and the page's own JavaScript creates the bug. PortSwigger's definition: it arises when JavaScript takes data from an attacker-controllable source, such as the URL, and passes it to a sink that supports dynamic code execution, such as `eval()` or `innerHTML`. *DOM* is the Document Object Model, the live tree of the page that scripts edit (prerequisite course). The class was named by Amit Klein, a security researcher, in a July 2005 paper, as [OWASP's DOM XSS page](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/DOM_Based_XSS) records.

Common **sources**: `location.search` (the `?query`), `location.hash` (the `#fragment`), `document.referrer`, `window.name`, and data received through `postMessage`. Common **sinks**: `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML()`, `document.write()`, `eval()`, string arguments to `setTimeout()` and `setInterval()`, and navigation such as `location = value` or `href` attributes, which run `javascript:` URLs.

blocks.title: One URL parameter, two versions of the same function

scenes.caption: The victim opens a link to the real site: /welcome?user= followed by an img tag with an onerror attribute. The page script starts reading the URL.
innerHTML hands the string to the HTML parser. It builds an img element with src=x and an onerror attribute, inside the heading.
Loading src=x fails, so the browser fires the error event and runs the onerror code as page script. The source reached a sink: DOM XSS.
scenes.output: alert(1) runs with the site's origin

scenes.caption: The fixed function reads the same parameter. Nothing has changed yet: the data is still attacker-controlled.
textContent creates one text node and never invokes the HTML parser. The heading shows the characters literally and no element is created.

blocks.md:
A detail that surprises people: a `<script>` element inserted through `innerHTML` does **not** run. PortSwigger notes this for all modern browsers, and a quick test in jsdom (a JavaScript implementation of the DOM) agrees. That is why the example uses an image with an `onerror` handler: event-handler attributes on inserted elements do fire. So "we block script tags" is not a defence for DOM sinks either.

`document.write()` is different: it does run script elements it writes. And `eval()`, `new Function()` and string `setTimeout()` need no HTML at all, because they run their argument as JavaScript directly.

The URL fragment (everything after `#`) is never sent to the server, as MDN's URL guide notes. A DOM XSS that reads `location.hash` leaves no trace in access logs and is invisible to a WAF. It has to be found in the JavaScript itself, by code review, by tests, or by browser-side tools such as DOM Invader, a tool preinstalled as an extension in Burp Suite's built-in browser that tracks sources reaching sinks.

blocks.caption: OWASP's DOM XSS rule: populate the DOM using safe JavaScript functions or properties.

blocks.md:
Libraries add their own sinks. PortSwigger's examples come from jQuery, a long-popular library that simplifies DOM scripting: its `$()` selector, which builds HTML when passed a string that looks like markup, and `.attr("href", ...)` with a URL taken from `location`, which can receive a `javascript:` URL. The rule is the same: know which functions parse HTML, run code or navigate, and never feed them unvalidated data.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: text sinks by default; an HTML sanitiser where HTML is genuinely needed (lesson 7); Trusted Types to make the browser refuse strings at sinks (lesson 8). *Detect*: server logs are blind to fragments, so rely on CSP and Trusted Types violation reports, which the browser sends from where the bug runs. *Respond*: ship the fixed script, and because cached copies of old JavaScript linger, consider versioned file names so every client gets the fix.

blocks.question: A single-page app reads `location.hash`, decodes it and assigns it to `innerHTML` to show a help topic. The team's WAF has never logged an attack on it. Why is that weak evidence?
options: WAFs only inspect POST bodies
innerHTML payloads are encrypted by the browser
The fragment after # is never sent to the server, so the WAF never sees that input at all
WAFs ignore requests from logged-in users
blocks.explain: Browsers keep the fragment on the client. The server and anything in front of it see only the path and query. DOM XSS through the hash is invisible to network defences and must be prevented in the code.

blocks.question: Which line contains a DOM XSS sink if `name` comes from the URL?
options: `el.textContent = name`
`el.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", name)`
`el.setAttribute("title", name)`
`document.createTextNode(name)`
blocks.explain: insertAdjacentHTML parses its argument as HTML, exactly like innerHTML. The other three create or set text and never run the HTML parser on the value.

lessons.title: Context decides the encoding: body, attribute, JavaScript, URL

blocks.md:
"Escape the output" sounds like one rule. It is really four or five, because, as OWASP puts it, browsers parse HTML, JavaScript, URLs and CSS differently, and using the wrong encoding can leave a hole or break the page. The **context** is where in the response the value lands, and it decides which characters are dangerous. Start with the one you have seen. In the **HTML body** (between tags such as `

` and `

`), the dangerous characters are the ones that start or end markup. The animation encodes a short attacker string with the `escapeHtml` function from lesson 2, character by character.

blocks.title: HTML-encoding a string, one character at a time

scenes.caption: Input as typed. A quote, a closing bracket and an opening bracket are exactly what an attacker needs to leave an attribute and start a new tag.
Quote becomes " and the angle brackets become > and <. Inside an element or a quoted attribute, these can no longer end or start anything.
Letters pass through unchanged. The ampersand becomes & so text that merely looks like an entity is shown literally rather than decoded.
The browser decodes each reference back to one visible character inside a text node. The user sees exactly what was typed; the page structure is unchanged.

blocks.md:
**Attribute context.** OWASP's rule: always quote attribute values, encode the value with an attribute encoder, and keep attribute *names* fixed. OWASP explains why quoting matters: in an unquoted attribute such as `<div class={{ c }}>` whitespace ends the value, so input such as `x onmouseover=...` adds a new attribute without needing a single special character. Event-handler attributes (`onclick` and friends) are a trap: the HTML parser decodes entities *before* the JavaScript runs, so HTML-encoding alone does not protect the JavaScript inside them. Attach handlers with `addEventListener()` instead.

**JavaScript context.** Putting data inside an inline `<script>` is the hardest case. PortSwigger explains that the browser runs the HTML parser first, to find where each script block ends, and only then runs the JavaScript parser. So a `</script>` *inside a JavaScript string* still ends the block. OWASP lists script blocks among its "dangerous contexts" and asks for an encoder made for both layers, or better, no untrusted data there at all.

blocks.caption: Outputs captured from Node 22. The dataset value comes back already decoded, as plain text.

blocks.md:
**URL context.** Two different problems hide here.

1. A value placed *inside* a URL, such as a query parameter: percent-encode it with `encodeURIComponent()`, which turns `a b&c=<d>` into `a%20b%26c%3D%3Cd%3E`, then HTML-attribute-encode the whole URL if it sits in an attribute (OWASP's "common mistake" section).
2. A whole URL from a user, such as a profile website link: no encoding helps, because `javascript:alert(1)` contains no special characters. You must parse it and allow only the schemes you expect, normally `https:` and `http:`.

**CSS context.** OWASP's advice is not to put untrusted data into CSS at all; when styling must depend on data, set one property through `element.style.setProperty()` with a value chosen from an allowlist.

blocks.title: One value, four contexts, four different defences

scenes.caption: The same user-supplied value can land in different parts of a page. The browser applies a different parser to each, so each needs its own treatment.
Between tags: HTML entity encoding of & < > " ' is enough. This is what template engines do by default.
Inside a quoted attribute such as title: attribute encoding with the quotes always present. Never inside on* handler attributes.
Inside a script block: the HTML parser can end the block early. Avoid it; pass data in a data- attribute or fetch it as JSON.
As a whole URL in href or src: encoding cannot stop a javascript: scheme. Parse and allow https: and http: only.

blocks.caption: Results from Node 22. Parse with the same URL rules the browser uses, never with a string prefix test.

blocks.prompt: A template auto-escapes HTML and renders `<a href="{{ website }}">`. A user sets their website to `javascript:alert(1)`. Does the link run script when clicked?
blocks.reveal: Yes. HTML escaping changes only `& < > " '`, and this value contains none of them, so it is output unchanged and the browser treats it as a `javascript:` URL. The context here is *URL*, not HTML text, and the defence is a scheme allowlist like `safeHref` above. Vue's security guide calls out this exact case, and OWASP's summary lists "untrusted URL in a src or href attribute" as needing URL validation in addition to attribute encoding.

blocks.question: A server template writes `<script>const name = <%- JSON.stringify(user.name) %>;</script>`. A user sets their name to a string containing `</script>`. What happens?
options: The HTML parser ends the script block at the `</script>` inside the string, and whatever follows is parsed as HTML
Nothing, because JSON.stringify escapes every special character
The JavaScript engine throws a syntax error, so no harm is done
The browser decodes the string twice and shows it in the page
blocks.explain: The HTML parser decides where a script block ends before JavaScript parsing starts, and it does not understand JavaScript strings. JSON.stringify leaves `<` and `/` alone. Escape `<` as a Unicode escape, or keep untrusted data out of inline scripts.

blocks.question: Why does OWASP say to quote every attribute value even after encoding?
options: Unquoted values cannot be encoded
Quotes make the attribute faster to parse
An unquoted value ends at whitespace, so input with a space can add new attributes such as event handlers without any special character
Browsers reject unquoted attributes in HTTPS pages
blocks.explain: With no quotes, a space ends the value and the rest of the input is read as new attributes. Encoders often leave spaces alone, so quoting is what keeps the value in one piece.

lessons.title: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches

blocks.md:
Writing `escapeHtml` by hand everywhere is how bugs like TweetDeck's happen. Modern frameworks (libraries that build the page's HTML for you; Django is a Python one for servers) invert the default. OWASP notes that apps built with modern frameworks have fewer XSS bugs because templating and auto-escaping steer developers the right way, and it recommends escaping every value by default rather than deciding which data is untrusted. - **React** encodes values embedded in JSX (HTML-like markup written inside JavaScript). MDN's example: `
Hello, {props.name}!
` with a name containing an `img` tag renders the tag as visible text. - **Vue** escapes `{{ }}` content and `:attr` bindings. Its guide notes this is done with native browser APIs such as `textContent` and `setAttribute`, so a hole would have to be a browser bug. - **Angular** treats all values as untrusted by default, and when you bind to `[innerHTML]` it *sanitises* the value rather than inserting it raw. - **Django** templates convert `< > ' " &` to entities automatically.

blocks.title: The default path versus the escape hatch

scenes.caption: A comment string arrives in a React component. On the default path, JSX puts it in a text node: the HTML parser never sees it.
The escape hatch: dangerouslySetInnerHTML assigns the string to the element's innerHTML, which runs the HTML parser on it.
Any markup in the string becomes real elements, including event-handler attributes. Auto-escaping did not fail; the code opted out of it.
Opting out safely: run the string through a sanitiser first. Only an allowlisted subset of HTML reaches innerHTML.

blocks.md:
Every framework also has an **escape hatch**, a way to insert raw HTML when you really need it, and that is where framework XSS lives. OWASP's list includes React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, Angular's `bypassSecurityTrust...` functions and Lit's `unsafeHTML` (Lit is a small library for building web components); add Vue's `v-html` and Django's `|safe` filter. The names are deliberately alarming. React's documentation says that unless the markup comes from a completely trusted source, it is trivial to introduce an XSS vulnerability this way.

The other gap is **URLs**. Auto-escaping a value does not validate it, so `<a :href="userUrl">` or `<a href={user.site}>` can still carry `javascript:`. Vue's guide calls this out; OWASP notes that React 19 blocks `javascript:` URLs in `src` and `href` but that this does not replace your own URL validation. Vue also warns that user-controlled `:style` can be used to lay a transparent link over your login button, a clickjacking-style trick inside your own page.

blocks.caption: safeHref is the scheme allowlist from lesson 5. If you only need text, use {user.bio} and skip HTML entirely.

blocks.md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: make the escape hatches rare and reviewable. A simple search for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `v-html`, `bypassSecurityTrust`, `|safe`, `innerHTML` and `insertAdjacentHTML` finds nearly all of them, and many teams make such a search (or a lint rule) a required review step. Every hit should either feed a sanitiser or carry a comment explaining why the data is safe. *Detect*: these sinks are client-side, so CSP and Trusted Types reports are the signal; React passes a `TrustedHTML` object through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` unchanged, so Trusted Types enforcement covers it (lesson 8). *Respond*: patch the component, then check whether stored content already contains payloads.

blocks.question:
A Vue app renders a bio with `

{{ user.bio }}

` and a link with ``. Which is the XSS risk?
options: The paragraph, because {{ }} inserts raw HTML
Neither, because Vue escapes both
Both, because Vue does no escaping in production builds
The link, because escaping does not stop a javascript: URL
blocks.explain: {{ }} uses textContent, so the bio is text. The :href binding is attribute-escaped, which stops breaking out of the attribute, but a value of javascript:... needs no special characters. Validate the scheme.

blocks.question: An Angular developer calls `bypassSecurityTrustHtml(comment)` because the sanitiser was removing a `style` attribute users wanted. What changed?
options: Nothing, because Angular still sanitises behind the scenes
Angular now inserts the comment without sanitising it, so any markup in it, including event handlers, reaches the DOM
Only styles are now allowed through
The comment is now encoded twice
blocks.explain: The bypass functions tell Angular a value is already safe, and Angular's docs say it then does not sanitise it. The fix for a missing feature is to configure a sanitiser to allow exactly what is needed, not to turn sanitisation off.

lessons.title: When users need HTML: sanitising with DOMPurify

blocks.md:
Encoding turns everything into text. That is wrong for a rich-text editor, a comment box that allows bold and links, or Markdown rendered to HTML: encoding would show the user `<b>` instead of **bold**. OWASP's answer for these cases is **HTML sanitisation**: strip the dangerous parts of the HTML and keep the safe parts. MDN defines it as removing unsafe features from a string of HTML, such as script tags or inline event handlers.

The widely recommended tool is **DOMPurify**, an open-source sanitiser for HTML, SVG and MathML started in February 2014 and published by Cure53, a Berlin security testing firm, under its `cure53` organisation on GitHub. OWASP and MDN both recommend it. Usage is one call: `DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty)` returns a clean string.

blocks.title: How an allowlist sanitiser cleans one comment

scenes.caption: The input string is parsed into a tree using the browser's own HTML parser, in an inert document where nothing loads or runs.
The sanitiser walks every element. div and img are on the allowlist of safe elements, so they stay.
script is not on the allowlist. The element and its contents are removed from the tree.
Attributes are checked too. src is allowed (and its URL checked); onerror is an event handler and is dropped.

What is left is serialised back to a string:
. That exact output came from DOMPurify 3.4.17 on this input.

blocks.caption: Outputs from DOMPurify 3.4.17 in Node 22 with jsdom. The javascript: link keeps its text but loses its href.

blocks.md:
**Why an allowlist, and why the browser's parser.** A sanitiser that searches the string with regular expressions has to predict how a browser will parse it, and Samy's worm showed how that goes: every deleted word had a parsing quirk that brought it back. DOMPurify lets the browser parse first, then inspects the real tree, keeping only known-safe elements and attributes. Its project keeps a public catalogue of the attack classes it defends against, such as *mutation XSS* (mXSS: markup that changes meaning when the sanitised result is parsed a second time) and *DOM clobbering* (allowed `id` and `name` attributes that overwrite variables the page's scripts read).

OWASP adds three pitfalls:

1. If you sanitise and then modify the result, you can void the protection.
2. If you pass sanitised HTML to a library that rewrites it, check that the library does not mutate it into something unsafe.
3. Keep the sanitiser patched: browsers change and bypasses are found.

Sanitise as the **last step before insertion**, in the context where it will be used. Sanitising on the server and then running the result through an emoji or link replacer in the browser re-opens the TweetDeck kind of bug: new HTML created after the check, never checked.

Browsers are now building this in. The **HTML Sanitizer API** adds `Element.setHTML()`, which MDN describes as an XSS-safe way to parse, sanitise and insert HTML: it always removes `script`, `frame`, `iframe`, `embed`, `object`, SVG `use` and event-handler attributes, even if a configuration allows them. DOMPurify's README says the project inspired the API. Check current browser support before relying on it, and keep a library fallback.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: one shared, configured sanitiser for the whole app, with the narrowest allowlist that meets the feature (a comment box rarely needs `style` or `iframe`). *Detect*: when stored HTML differs a lot from its sanitised form, someone tried something; logging the size of what was removed is a cheap signal. *Respond*: after a sanitiser bypass is announced, upgrade, then re-sanitise or re-render stored content, because content saved under the old version may already carry the payload.

blocks.question: A forum sanitises posts with DOMPurify, then replaces `:smile:` with ``. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because the post was already sanitised
DOMPurify does not allow img elements
Emoji images are blocked by every CSP
The replacement builds new HTML from user text after sanitising, so that text is never checked
blocks.explain: OWASP warns that modifying sanitised content can void the protection. Here user-controlled text is pasted into an attribute after the sanitiser ran. Run the replacement first and sanitise the final HTML, or build the emoji element with DOM APIs.

blocks.question: Why does DOMPurify parse the HTML with the browser's own parser instead of matching patterns in the string?
options: So that it inspects the same tree the browser will actually build, rather than guessing how the browser will read the string
Parsing is faster than regular expressions
Because regular expressions are not available in JavaScript
To convert the HTML to plain text
blocks.explain: Pattern filters fail when the browser parses the string differently from the filter's assumptions, as MySpace's did. Checking the real parsed tree removes that guesswork, which is why allowlist sanitisers built on the DOM are the recommended approach.

lessons.title: Second lines of defence: strict CSP and Trusted Types

blocks.md:
Encoding and sanitising aim to keep attacker code out of the page. The prerequisite course taught the backup: a **strict Content Security Policy** based on a per-response nonce (or hashes) plus `'strict-dynamic'`, `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`. The browser then runs only scripts the server vouched for in that response. Here is what such a policy does to each kind of XSS from this course:

- **Reflected or stored `<script>` tag**: blocked, because it carries no valid nonce.
- **Injected event handler**, such as an `img` with `onerror` arriving through `innerHTML`: blocked, because strict policies refuse inline handlers.
- **`javascript:` URLs**: blocked.
- **DOM XSS into `eval()` or string `setTimeout()`**: blocked, unless the policy adds `'unsafe-eval'`.

And what it does not stop:

- **HTML injection that runs no script**: a fake login form, or injected markup that leaks page text (PortSwigger calls this *dangling markup injection*). CSP is about loading and running resources, not about what HTML says.
- **Your own trusted script passing attacker data to a script-loading sink.** `'strict-dynamic'` deliberately extends trust to scripts that a trusted script creates. If your code does `s.src = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("plugin")`, the browser loads the attacker's URL as a trusted child.
- **A permissive policy.** With `'unsafe-inline'` and no nonce, most XSS runs.

So CSP narrows the attack surface a lot, but the DOM sinks of lesson 4 need their own guard. That guard is **Trusted Types**.

**Trusted Types** is a browser API, described on web.dev by Krzysztof Kotowicz, a Google engineer who edits the Trusted Types specification, that makes dangerous sinks refuse plain strings. MDN groups the sinks into three kinds, each with its own *trusted type*, an object that can only be made by code you approved:

- **HTML sinks** (`innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, iframe `srcdoc`, `DOMParser`) need a `TrustedHTML`.
- **JavaScript sinks** (`eval`, `new Function`, string `setTimeout`, script `text`) need a `TrustedScript`.
- **Script URL sinks** (`script.src`, `Worker()`, `importScripts`) need a `TrustedScriptURL`.

You create those objects through a **policy**: a named object with functions such as `createHTML(input)` that you write, typically wrapping DOMPurify. The CSP directive `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` turns enforcement on: after that, assigning a string to any of these sinks throws a `TypeError`. The API does not sanitise anything itself; it guarantees that your policy ran.

blocks.title: Trusted Types: strings are refused at the sink

scenes.caption: Without enforcement, a string from the URL flows straight into innerHTML, and the HTML parser builds whatever it contains.
With require-trusted-types-for 'script', the same assignment throws a TypeError. Nothing is parsed, and the browser sends a violation report.
The approved path: code passes the string through a named policy whose createHTML runs DOMPurify. The result is a TrustedHTML object.
The sink accepts the TrustedHTML. Only sanitised markup reaches the DOM, and every such path goes through a policy you can review.
The trusted-types directive lists allowed policy names. A third-party script trying to create its own permissive policy gets an exception.

blocks.caption: web.dev's strict CSP structure with the two Trusted Types directives added. Headers are one line in practice.
Based on MDN's Trusted Types examples. Run it in a browser that supports the API, with the header above.

blocks.md:
**Rolling it out.** web.dev's guide starts with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: require-trusted-types-for 'script'; report-to csp` so the browser reports every string-to-sink assignment without breaking anything. You then refactor each one to use text sinks or a policy. MDN also describes a **default policy**: a policy literally named `default` is called automatically for any string reaching a sink, which helps during migration, but MDN recommends it only as a transition step. MDN lists Trusted Types as Baseline "newly available" since February 2026, meaning current versions of all major browsers support it.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: strict CSP everywhere, Trusted Types on apps with heavy client-side rendering. *Detect*: both produce JSON violation reports; Trusted Types violations arrive with `effectiveDirective` set to `require-trusted-types-for`, which is what web.dev's `ReportingObserver` example filters on. *Respond*: a sudden cluster of reports from one page is an attack in progress or a regression, and either way it points to the exact line.
Trusted Types changes the review question from "is any of our thousands of DOM writes unsafe?" to "are our two or three policies correct?". The browser enforces that nothing else reaches a sink.

blocks.question: A page has a strict nonce CSP with 'strict-dynamic'. Its trusted app.js reads a `?widget=` URL parameter and does `s = document.createElement("script"); s.src = widget; document.body.append(s)`. Is the attacker's script blocked?
options: Yes, because it has no nonce
Yes, because 'strict-dynamic' blocks all dynamically created scripts
No, because 'strict-dynamic' trusts scripts created by an already-trusted script, so this needs Trusted Types or a code fix
No, because CSP never applies to script elements
blocks.explain: 'strict-dynamic' exists so trusted loaders can add scripts without listing every host. The cost is that a trusted script with a DOM XSS bug can load anything. A TrustedScriptURL policy, or simply not taking script URLs from user input, closes it.

blocks.question: A team enables `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` and creates a policy whose createHTML returns its input unchanged. What protection do they have?
options: Full protection, since every sink now requires a TrustedHTML
Little: strings still reach innerHTML, just through a named function. Trusted Types guarantees the policy ran, not that it is safe
The browser sanitises TrustedHTML values automatically
None, because the policy will be rejected by the browser
blocks.explain: MDN is explicit that the API supplies no sanitiser. A pass-through policy adds visibility (one place to review) but no safety. The policy has to sanitise, typically with DOMPurify.

lessons.title: CSRF: making the victim's browser send the request

blocks.md:
XSS puts attacker code *inside* your origin. **Cross-site request forgery** (CSRF) never gets inside at all. MDN's definition: an attacker tricks the user's browser into making an HTTP request to the target site from a malicious site; the request includes the user's credentials, and the server carries out a harmful action, thinking the user intended it. The name says it: a *request* that is *forged* (made without the user's intent), sent *cross-site* from the attacker's page. OWASP lists other names you will meet: XSRF, "Sea Surf", session riding, cross-site reference forgery, hostile linking, and Microsoft's term, one-click attack.

Tiny example: you are logged in to your bank. In another tab you open a page about kittens. That page contains a hidden form that posts `recipient=attacker&amount=1000` to your bank, and a line of script that submits it as soon as the page loads.

Why does this work? Recall two facts from the prerequisite course. The same-origin policy blocks *reading* cross-origin responses but generally allows *sending* requests, such as form posts. And the browser attaches cookies by destination: a request to `bank.example` carries `bank.example`'s cookies, whoever started it, unless `SameSite` says otherwise.

MDN lists the conditions for CSRF. The site:

1. uses HTTP requests to change state on the server (a **state-changing request**),
2. relies only on cookies to tell which user sent it, and
3. uses only request parameters an attacker can predict.

The attacker never sees the response, and does not need to: the money has already moved.

blocks.caption: A forged cross-site POST to this handler succeeded in a local test (HTTP 200). Changing the email lets the attacker reset the password next.

blocks.code:
<!-- On the attacker's page (MDN's textbook illustration) -->
<form action="https://app.example/account/email" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@mail.example">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit();</script>
blocks.caption: The form submits on page load. A hidden iframe can host it so the victim sees nothing change.

blocks.title: A forged request, then the same request against a defended site

scenes.caption: The victim logged in to app.example earlier, so their browser holds app.example's session cookie.
Later the victim opens an attacker's page. It returns the hidden form and the auto-submit script.
The form posts to app.example. The browser attaches app.example's cookie because that is where the request goes. The attacker's page never sees it.
The vulnerable handler sees a valid session and changes the email. The attacker cannot read this response, and does not need to.
Defended site: the session cookie is SameSite=Lax, so a cross-site POST goes out without it. Separately, the handler demands a token the attacker could not read.

blocks.caption: In the local test the forged request got 403 (cross-site blocked), a same-origin request without the token got 403, and one with the token got 200.

blocks.md: **Variants worth knowing.** - **GET actions.** If a state change happens on GET, the attacker needs no form: MDN's example is an `` whose `src` is the transfer URL. Loading the page fires the request. - **"JSON" APIs that accept simple content types.** A cross-site form can only send `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data` or `text/plain`. OWASP warns that an API which also accepts `text/plain` and parses the body as JSON is open to CSRF. - **Login CSRF.** OWASP describes forging a *login* request so the victim is signed in to the attacker's account; anything they then enter, such as card details, lands in the attacker's account. Login forms need protection too. - **WebSocket handshakes.** The handshake is an ordinary GET that carries cookies, so if the server accepts it on cookies alone without checking `Origin` or a token, a cross-site page can open a socket as the victim and, unlike a form, read the replies. PortSwigger calls this cross-site WebSocket hijacking.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: the next lesson. *Detect*: CSRF arrives as an ordinary authenticated request, so look at the headers the browser adds, which a page cannot forge: an `Origin` naming a site you do not own, `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on a state-changing endpoint, and a burst of the same action (email or password change) across many users soon after a link circulated. Log token failures as security events, as OWASP recommends. *Respond*: reverse the forged changes (for example, restore account emails and force password resets), and add the missing defence.

blocks.question: A victim visits an attacker's page that auto-submits a form to `https://bank.example/transfer`. The same-origin policy is working normally. Why does the transfer happen?
options: The policy blocks reading cross-origin responses, not sending requests, and the browser attaches the bank's cookies to a request addressed to the bank
The same-origin policy does not apply to HTTPS sites
The attacker's page stole the cookie first
Forms are a type of CORS request that the bank approved
blocks.explain: Cross-origin form submission is a write, which the web has allowed since the beginning. Cookies follow the destination. The forged request looks exactly like a real one unless the server checks something the attacker cannot supply.

blocks.question: Which endpoint is NOT a CSRF risk, even with cookie-only authentication?
options: POST /settings/email
GET /logout that ends the session
GET /api/search?q= that only reads and returns public results
POST /api/orders accepting text/plain bodies parsed as JSON
blocks.explain: CSRF lets an attacker cause an action; they cannot read the response. A read-only endpoint returning public data gives them nothing. GET /logout changes state (a nuisance-level CSRF), and the text/plain JSON API is OWASP's example of a simple-request CSRF hole.

lessons.title: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata

blocks.md:
CSRF works because a cookie proves *who* is asking but not *where the request came from*. Every defence adds that second fact. OWASP's order of advice: use your framework's built-in protection if it has one; otherwise use **tokens** for state-changing requests; for modern browsers, **Fetch Metadata** headers are a strong primary check with an `Origin` fallback; and `SameSite` cookies add depth. Never change state on GET.

**SameSite**, recalled from the prerequisite: `Lax` keeps cookies off cross-site requests except top-level GET navigations; `Strict` keeps them off all cross-site requests. OWASP and MDN list its limits:

- `Lax` still sends the cookie on cross-site GET navigations, so any state-changing GET is exposed.
- SameSite is scoped to the **site**, not the origin: a request from a compromised `blog.example.com` counts as same-site for `app.example.com`.
- Browser defaults differ, so set it explicitly.
- It does nothing against attacks from inside your own origin.

blocks.title: Which defence stops which forgery? (1 = blocked, 0 = gets through)

scenes.caption: Rows are attacks, columns are single defences, each applied to the targeted endpoint. Read across a row to see what a given attack defeats.
A classic cross-site form POST is stopped by every defence on its own.

A state-changing GET reached by a top-level link: Lax sends the cookie on that navigation, and a Fetch Metadata policy that checks only unsafe methods, as OWASP's does, lets it through too. Strict and a token stop it.
A POST from a compromised sibling subdomain is same-site, so both SameSite values send the cookie. It is still cross-origin, so tokens and a same-origin Fetch Metadata check stop it.
Script running inside your origin (XSS) can read tokens and makes same-origin requests. No CSRF defence stops it, which is OWASP's warning in one row.

blocks.md:
**Synchronizer tokens.** OWASP calls the *synchronizer token pattern* one of the most popular and recommended defences. The server generates a token per session (or per request), stores it in the session, and embeds it in each form as a hidden field or sends it for JavaScript to put in a custom header. Every state-changing request must return it, and the server compares. The token must be unique per session, secret and unpredictable (a large random value from a secure generator). It works because a cross-site page cannot read your pages, so it cannot learn the token. OWASP adds that the token should not travel in the URL, where it leaks into logs and `Referer` headers.

For stateless servers OWASP recommends a **signed double-submit cookie**: the token is an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code: a hash made with a server secret key) over a session-bound value, set in a cookie and also sent in a header or form field. The plain double-submit version without signing is discouraged, because an attacker who can write cookies on your domain can plant a matching pair.

blocks.caption: Exercised against Express 5 in the previous lesson's test. timingSafeEqual avoids leaking the token through comparison time.

blocks.md:
**Origin and Fetch Metadata.** Browsers add headers that page script cannot set (they are on the Fetch standard's *forbidden header* list). `Origin` names the origin that started the request. `Sec-Fetch-Site` states the relationship directly: `same-origin`, `same-site`, `cross-site`, or `none` for user-typed navigations. OWASP notes `Sec-Fetch-*` has been supported in all major browsers since March 2023, recommends rejecting unsafe methods when the value is `cross-site`, and treating `same-site` with suspicion unless you trust every sibling subdomain. Go 1.25 ships this check in its standard library as `CrossOriginProtection`. Missing headers or `Origin: null` are not evidence of a same-origin request.

**APIs called by JavaScript** can rely on the fact that a custom header (such as `X-CSRF-Token`) or `Content-Type: application/json` makes the request non-simple, so a cross-origin page triggers a CORS preflight that your server will refuse. MDN notes the catch: a CORS policy that allows the attacker's origin with credentials re-opens CSRF.

Cross-site scripting defeats every CSRF defence, as the Samy worm showed by reading MySpace's token. CSRF defences assume the attacker is outside your origin. Fix XSS first; then CSRF defences mean something.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: framework CSRF middleware on, `__Host-` session cookie with `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict` for high-value actions), a Fetch Metadata check, and no state change on GET. Re-authenticate for the most sensitive actions (password, payout details), as OWASP suggests. *Detect*: count 403s from the token and Fetch Metadata checks by endpoint and by `Origin`; a rise naming one foreign site is an attack, a rise naming your own origin is a bug you just shipped. *Respond*: block the foreign origin at the edge while you review, and reverse any changes that slipped through before the defence was in place.

blocks.question: A bank sets its session cookie to `SameSite=Lax` and does nothing else. Its old endpoint `GET /transfer?to=...&amount=...` moves money. Is it protected?
options: Yes, Lax blocks all cross-site requests
Yes, because GET requests cannot change state
No, because SameSite only works over HTTP/2
No, because Lax still sends the cookie on a cross-site top-level GET navigation, such as a link the victim clicks
blocks.explain: Lax was designed to keep links into your site working, so it sends cookies on top-level GET navigations. That makes state-changing GETs the most common way SameSite-only defences fail, according to OWASP.

blocks.question: A server puts its CSRF token only in a cookie and checks that the cookie is present on each POST. Why does this not help?
options: Cookies are encrypted, so the server cannot read the token
The browser attaches the cookie to the forged request automatically, so its presence proves nothing about where the request came from
Tokens must be at least 512 bits long
The attacker can read the cookie through the same-origin policy
blocks.explain: A token only works when the request must carry it in a place the attacker cannot fill: a form field or header. OWASP says cookie-only validation is insecure for exactly this reason.

blocks.question: app.example.com uses `SameSite=Strict` cookies. An attacker takes over the forgotten subdomain `promo.example.com`. What stops a forged POST from promo to app?
options: Strict already blocks it, because the hosts differ
HSTS on app.example.com
Nothing can stop it
A CSRF token or a Sec-Fetch-Site check that requires same-origin, because the request is same-site but cross-origin
blocks.explain: SameSite compares sites, and both hosts share the site example.com, so the cookie is sent. The request is still cross-origin, so promo cannot read app's pages to learn a token, and the browser reports Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site, which a same-origin-only check rejects.

blocks.md:
Many sites send you somewhere after an action: `/login?next=/orders` returns you to your orders after you sign in. If the site redirects to *any* value of `next`, it has an **open redirect**: an endpoint that will forward visitors to an address the attacker chooses. OWASP's cheat sheet calls these *unvalidated redirects and forwards*.

On its own it runs no script, so why care? Because the link starts on your real domain. PortSwigger notes that an authentic application URL with a valid TLS certificate lends credibility to a phishing attack, since users who check the domain see yours. Redirects also appear inside sign-in flows, where sending a user to the wrong place can carry more than a page view.

blocks.caption: Both send the visitor to an attacker's page from a link that starts with the real domain.

scenes.caption: The attacker emails a link. The visible host is the real shop, and the certificate on the first hop will be valid.
The victim checks the domain, sees shop.example, and clicks. The real shop receives the request.
The shop answers with a redirect to whatever next says. The browser follows it without asking.
The look-alike login page collects the password. The user arrived through a link they had verified.
With safeNext, the shop only redirects within its own origin. The same link lands on the shop's home page.

blocks.title: safeNext on five inputs

scenes.caption: A normal relative path resolves against the shop's origin. Same origin, so it is allowed.
A full URL to another host parses fine but has a different origin, so the visitor goes home instead.
Protocol-relative //evil.example looks like a path to a naive startsWith("/") check. The URL parser sees host evil.example.
A look-alike host that begins with the real name fails, because origins are compared whole, not by prefix.
A javascript: URL has an opaque origin, written as the string null, so it can never equal BASE.

blocks.md:
**Why the fix works.** It does what OWASP asks: parse with a real URL parser, compare the parsed scheme, host and port (the origin) with an exact allowlist, and redirect to the parsed result rather than the raw string. Returning the absolute `u.href` matters: returning only the path could hand back `//evil.example` for an input like `https://shop.example//evil.example`, and a browser would read that as a link to another host. All five outputs above, plus that case, were checked in Node 22.

OWASP's other options are even safer when they fit: avoid redirects that take a URL at all, or accept a short ID (`?next=orders`) that the server maps to a fixed URL. If you must send users to other sites, show an interstitial page naming the destination. A DOM redirect needs the same check, and more urgently: PortSwigger notes that if the attacker controls the start of the URL, `location = value` with a `javascript:` URL is not a redirect but DOM XSS.

**Clickjacking, revisited.** The prerequisite course covered the mechanism in full: an attacker's page loads your page in a transparent frame and lines up your real button under their decoy, so the victim's click lands on your page. It acts as the victim only if the frame is logged in, which needs the session cookie sent to a cross-site frame (`SameSite=None`); `Lax` and `Strict` cookies are withheld there, as the prerequisite showed. The defence is a response header, `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (or a short list of origins allowed to frame you), plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY` for older browsers.

Two points belong with this course. First, clickjacking is CSRF's cousin: both make the browser perform an authenticated action the user did not intend, but clickjacking uses a real click, so CSRF tokens do not help (the framed page includes its own valid token). Second, Vue's security guide shows a variant *inside* your own page: if users control a `style` binding, they can place a transparent link over your login button.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: allowlist redirects as above; `frame-ancestors` on every HTML response; never bind user input to `style`. *Detect*: log every redirect decision where `next` was rejected; a run of rejections pointing to one foreign host means a phishing campaign is using your domain. Mail filters and user reports often flag the campaign first. *Respond*: the fix is a code change; also tell your security contact and abuse desk the attacker's domain so it can be reported for takedown.

blocks.question: A developer validates `next` with `next.startsWith("/")`. Which input still sends users off-site?
options: //evil.example/login
/orders
/account/settings
/?ref=email
blocks.explain: Two leading slashes form a protocol-relative URL: the browser keeps the current scheme and treats evil.example as the host. Parsing with new URL() and comparing the origin catches it, because the parser and the browser agree.

blocks.question: Why do CSRF tokens not stop clickjacking?
options: Clickjacking only targets GET requests
Tokens are removed when a page is framed
The attacker frames the real page, which includes its own valid token, and the victim's real click submits it
Clickjacking uses the attacker's own cookies
blocks.explain: In clickjacking the forged action is performed by your genuine page, inside a frame, with a genuine click. Everything it sends is legitimate, token included. Only refusing to be framed (frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options) stops it.

lessons.title: Third-party scripts and Magecart: British Airways and polyfill.io

blocks.md:
Every `<script src>` on your page runs with your origin's full power, whoever wrote it and wherever it is hosted (prerequisite, lesson 1). That makes a script supplier, or anyone who can change a script file you serve, as powerful as an XSS attacker, with no injection bug needed. RiskIQ, a threat-intelligence firm, counted around 20 scripts on British Airways' main page in 2018 and 30 on the booking page, many minified (whitespace and long names stripped to shrink the file, which also makes it hard to read) and thousands of lines long.

The best-known abuse is **Magecart**: criminals who insert code into checkout pages to copy card details as customers type them. Sansec, a firm that hunts these attacks, [explains the name](https://sansec.io/what-is-magecart) as a blend of *Magento* (an e-commerce platform that dominated online shops when the crime took off) and *shopping cart*. It is also called **web skimming** or **formjacking**, by analogy with card skimmers hidden in ATMs.

**Real case: British Airways (August to September 2018).** BA announced on 6 September 2018 that payments made through its website and app between 22:58 on 21 August and 21:45 on 5 September, BST (British Summer Time) had been compromised. RiskIQ researcher Yonathan Klijnsma reconstructed it from the firm's web crawls:

- The attackers modified a copy of the **Modernizr** library (a feature-detection script, version 2.6.2) served from BA's own site, appending code at the bottom so it kept working.
- The clean file's `Last-Modified` header dated from December 2012; the modified one matched the start of the breach.
- The added code was 22 lines. When a customer released the mouse or lifted a finger (`mouseup`, `touchend`) on the payment button, it copied the payment form and the payer's name and sent them as JSON to the look-alike `baways.com`.
- That server had a paid TLS certificate issued on 15 August, six days before the skimming began.
- BA's mobile app loaded parts of the website, including the same Modernizr file, so app users were hit too; the `touchend` handler covered them.

blocks.title: British Airways 2018, in days from 15 August

scenes.caption: 15 August: a TLS certificate is issued for baways.com, the attackers' collection server. RiskIQ took this as a sign they had access before the reported start.
21 August, 22:58 BST (day 6.96): the modified Modernizr starts skimming payment forms on the website and in the app.
The skimmer runs for 14.95 days, until 21:45 BST on 5 September (day 21.91). Every payment in that window is copied.
6 September (day 22): BA announces the breach. 11 September (day 27): RiskIQ publishes how 22 lines of code did it, found by watching for a changed script.

blocks.title: Where the card data went, and where a policy could have stopped it

scenes.caption: The customer types card details into BA's real payment form, on BA's real domain, over HTTPS. Nothing looks wrong.
Modernizr is a first-party file, loaded by BA's own page. The appended lines run with BA's origin and can read every field.
On mouseup or touchend, the form is serialised and sent as JSON to baways.com. Sending data cross-origin is a write; the same-origin policy allows it.
Simplified what-if: a CSP connect-src listing only BA's payment hosts would have refused the request to baways.com and sent a report, unless the attackers could also change BA's headers.

blocks.md:
BA first put the number affected at around 380,000; the UK Information Commissioner's Office later fined it GBP 20 million for a breach affecting more than 400,000 customers ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-54568784)). The file was BA's own, so SRI on third-party tags would not have helped, and a CSP trusting `'self'` would have run it. What helps is knowing which scripts the payment page loads and noticing when one changes, which is how RiskIQ found it.

**Real case: polyfill.io (2024).** The prerequisite course told the outline: a company bought the `polyfill.io` domain and GitHub account in February 2024, and by June the CDN was injecting malicious code. Sansec's report adds detail: the code was generated per request from HTTP headers, ran only on certain mobile devices at certain hours, stayed quiet for admin users, and delayed itself when web analytics was present. It redirected some visitors to betting sites via a fake analytics domain. Sansec later tied the same actor to other script CDNs used since at least June 2023.

The response shows the ecosystem's levers. Cloudflare had mirrored the library on its cdnjs service in February out of concern about the sale, and in June began rewriting `polyfill.io` links to its mirror at its edge for sites it proxied. Google started blocking ads for e-commerce sites that used polyfill.io, and the domain's registrar, Namecheap, put the domain on hold. The original author's advice was to remove it: modern browsers no longer need it.

The lesson: a **domain's owner is part of your code**. When the owner changes, your code changes, with no commit in your repository.

blocks.caption: A toy version of RiskIQ's method. Real monitors render the page in a browser, because scripts also add scripts at runtime.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: keep payment and login pages nearly script-free; self-host and pin what you need, with SRI for anything static from a third party; strict CSP with a tight `connect-src` (and `form-action`) so data cannot leave for a new host; and consider taking card entry off your page entirely, into a payment provider's hosted field or page, so your scripts never see card numbers. *Detect*: CSP reports naming a new destination; external monitoring that loads the page as a customer would and alerts when any script's content or any outbound host changes; file-integrity monitoring on the web servers. *Respond*: remove or pin the script, find how the file was changed (BA's attackers had access to its servers), tell the card brands and affected customers, and meet breach-notification deadlines.

blocks.question: Why would Subresource Integrity on BA's third-party tags not have stopped the 2018 skimmer?
options: SRI does not work on payment pages
The modified file was served by BA itself, by attackers who had access to BA's systems, so they could change both the file and any integrity value
SRI only checks stylesheets
Modernizr is too large to hash
blocks.explain: SRI protects you from a change on someone else's server. Here the file was first-party and the attackers controlled what BA served. Change detection on the page, plus a connect-src policy limiting where data can go, target this case.

blocks.question: polyfill.io's code was generated per request and changed by device and time. What does that imply for detection?
options: A single scan from a desktop office network might see a clean file, so monitoring has to vary devices and times, and CSP reports from real users matter
Any single fetch of the file will reveal the malware
SRI hashes would have caught it on every request
Server logs on the sites that embedded it show the injected code
blocks.explain: Selective payloads are designed to evade the checks defenders usually run. Reports from real browsers (CSP violations when the redirect domain is not allowed) and monitoring that imitates real users are what see them. Sites embedding a third-party script never receive its body in their own logs.

lessons.title: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page

blocks.md:
A **browser extension** is a small program installed into the browser that adds features: a password manager, an ad blocker, a grammar checker. Many of them need to see the pages you visit, and that makes them the client side's biggest blind spot. You did not ship their code, your CSP and code review never saw it, and it may run on your site in your users' browsers.

Chrome's documentation describes the two pieces that matter. **Content scripts** are files that run in the context of web pages; using the standard DOM they can read details of the pages the browser visits and change them. They run in an **isolated world**, a private JavaScript environment, so their variables are separate from the page's, but they share the same DOM: every form field, every token in the HTML. **Host permissions** declare which sites an extension may touch, from one domain to every site.

blocks.caption: Chrome's manifest format. Chrome warns users about host permissions at install, and changes to them can trigger new warnings.

blocks.title: How a trusted extension turned hostile overnight

nodes.label:
Sites the user
is logged in to

scenes.caption: A legitimate extension is installed by many users, with permission to read pages. Its updates come from the developer's account on the store.

A phishing email gets a developer to approve a malicious OAuth app (OAuth: the standard that lets a user give an app limited access to an account without sharing the password). The attacker gets publishing rights.
The attacker uploads a modified version. It passes the store's review and browsers update to it automatically.
On matching sites, the content script reads the page and the session, and sends tokens and cookies to the attacker's command server.

blocks.md:
**Real case: Cyberhaven (December 2024).** Cyberhaven, a data-security company, published its own analysis. On 24 December 2024 a phishing email reached the extension's public support address. Clicking it led into Google's standard authorisation flow for a malicious OAuth app named "Privacy Policy Extension", which gave the attacker the rights to publish. The attacker took a clean copy of the extension, added code, and uploaded it as version 24.10.4; it passed the Chrome Web Store's security review and replaced the real one for part of Cyberhaven's customers.

The added code fetched its configuration from a command server, then, when the user visited facebook.com while logged in, collected their Facebook access token, user ID, account, business and ad-account details, and cookies, and sent them out. Cyberhaven concluded it was part of a wider, non-targeted campaign against extension developers aimed at Facebook advertising accounts.

Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: for organisations, allow only reviewed extensions through browser management policy, prefer extensions that request narrow host permissions, and restrict and review which third-party OAuth apps may access developer and publisher accounts. Strong sign-in did not help: Cyberhaven says its employee had MFA (multi-factor authentication) and Google Advanced Protection (sign-in only with a passkey or security key), got no MFA prompt, and still consented. For site owners, `HttpOnly` hides cookies from page script but not from an extension with the `cookies` permission (this one took Facebook cookies), so keep sessions short and re-authenticate high-value actions. *Detect*: inventory installed extensions and their versions across the fleet; alert when a widely installed one changes permissions or publisher; watch for sessions suddenly used from new locations. *Respond*: remove or disable the extension version centrally, end sessions and rotate credentials for sites it could reach, and review account activity, such as ad spend, during the window.

blocks.question: A user's banking session is used by an attacker. The bank finds no XSS, and its CSP is strict. A malicious browser extension with access to all sites is installed. Why did the bank's defences not help?
options: Extensions are exempt from HTTPS
CSP only applies to mobile browsers
The extension's content script runs in the user's browser with access to the page's DOM, outside anything the bank served or reviewed
The bank's cookies were not HttpOnly
blocks.explain: Content scripts read and change the page through the shared DOM. The bank's policies govern code the bank delivers; an extension the user installed is a separate principal with its own permissions.

blocks.question: In the Cyberhaven incident, what was the initial weakness the attacker used?
options: A buffer overflow in Chrome
A stolen password reused from another breach
An XSS bug in the Chrome Web Store
A phishing email that got a developer to approve a malicious OAuth application with publishing rights
blocks.explain: Cyberhaven's analysis describes a phishing email leading into Google's normal authorisation flow for an app called Privacy Policy Extension. Consent to a malicious app is enough; no password was needed. Reviewing and restricting OAuth grants is part of the defence.

lessons.title: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks

blocks.md:
Client-side attacks are hard to see because they run in browsers you do not own. The trick is to know which sensor sees which attack:

- **CSP and Trusted Types violation reports** come from the browser itself, so they see everything that runs in the page: reflected, stored and DOM XSS, unexpected third-party destinations, sink misuse.
- **Access logs and a WAF** see requests: reflected payloads in query strings and stored payloads on their way in. They never see URL fragments or what a third-party script does.
- **Application logs** see CSRF: `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` values on state-changing endpoints, token failures, bursts of the same account change.
- **External script monitoring** sees silent changes to what your pages load (the BA method).
- **Users and partners** report phishing pages and odd behaviour, often first.

scenes.caption: Five sensors around one web app. None of them sees every attack, so a team needs several.
Reflected XSS: the payload is in the URL, so the WAF and access logs see it; if it runs, CSP reports it from the browser.
DOM XSS through the fragment: the server never sees it. Only browser reports (CSP and Trusted Types) can.
CSRF: requests look normal to a WAF. Application logs of Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site and token failures carry the signal.
